newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein's Adams in first meeting with Mowlam.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein's Adams in first meeting with Mowlam.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, was due to hold his first formal talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary on Wednesday to pave the way for his party's historic entry into peace talks.

The meeting (1000 GMT) between the Sinn Fein president and Mo Mowlam, the British government's Northern Ireland minister, was taking place less than three weeks after Adams's IRA guerrilla allies called a halt to their guerrilla war for Irish reunification.

Mowlam was expected to tell Adams that Sinn Fein will be allowed into multi-party peace talks in September for the first time, providing the London government deems the Irish Republican Army ceasefire genuine and credible.

But she was likely to tell Adams that IRA targeting of potential victims and sites and so-called "punishment beatings" meted out by self-styled IRA police to wayward Catholics will be viewed as a breach of the guerrillas' July 20 ceasefire.

She was also expected to spell out that Northern Ireland will remain part of Britain so long as the majority -- currently 60 percent pro-British Protestant -- wants it to be, and that nothing will alter that.

There have been no IRA bomb or gun attacks since the guerrillas last month called an "unequivocal restoration" of a broken August 1994 ceasefire in a bid to get Sinn Fein to the negotiating table for the first time.
But the scenes of jubilation which greeted the first IRA truce were not repeated after July 20. Mowlam said this week that the 1.5 million population were "very wary and rightly so".

She is also keenly aware that Adams' entry into negotiations on a lasting settlement to a 28-year war which has killed 3,200 may provoke his pro-British unionist foes into refusing direct talks with him until the IRA is disarmed and disbanded.
Adams says his goal since 1993 has been to join the talks between Protestant unionists who want the province to remain in the United Kingdom and Irish Catholic nationalists.
But he was barred from the negotiations by their co-sponsors Britain and Ireland, and cast into the political wilderness until the July 20 ceasefire.

Northern Ireland's main pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist Party led by David Trimble, says it will not walk out of the negotiations but wants the IRA to hand over weapons to prove the truce is real and that its war is over for good.
Two smaller unionist parties walked out of the talks altogether in protest at Anglo-Irish proposals to allow guerrillas to disarm in stages as the political talks progress.
Adams says the IRA is sticking to its decades-old policy that "not a single bullet" will be surrendered until a final settlement is reached.

Adams's meeting with Mowlam will mark another step towards ending his vilification by successive British governments who banned his voice from the airwaves and barred him from Britain until the first IRA ceasefire in 1994.
Former British prime minister John Major once said the thought of negotiating with Sinn Fein would make him physically ill.

Adams's IRA backers came close to blowing up the entire British cabinet of prime minister Margaret Thatcher with a bomb in a Brighton hotel in 1984, and lobbed mortars into Major's central London residence at 10 Downing Street.

In recent weeks Adams has held talks with Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern. He is expected to meet senior Clinton administration officials on a visit to the United States in the first week of September.
